Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals. “We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post . “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link. Claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. model:vllm|title:encoder disaggregation.content_excerpt: Multimodal inference adds an encoding stage before language-model execution. Images, video frames, and audio must be processed into embeddings before the language model can use them. The demand on this stage varies with media size, modality, and request mix, and can change independently of prefill and decode demand. Encoder / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates these stages into independently deployed vLLM instances. Recent work in the vLLM community has expanded EPD across model execution, remote embedding transfer, shared caching, multimodal input handling, and request routing. DeepSeek's inference deployment Q&A describes an E/P/D architecture with a separately deployed vision encoder. vLLM has supported encoder disaggregation since our December 2025 architecture post , and continues to improve that support. vLLM main now also supports metadata-only EPD for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This post explains the engineering behind that progress, with a focus on five changes: The EPD tracker links the ongoing work. The core vLLM capabilities described below, including MiMo and XPU support, are included in vLLM v0.32.0. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash metadata-only support is available on main through #62802 . The vLLM Router and SMG integrations below use their respective main branches. EPD supports two deployment patterns: E+PD , with a separate encoder and a combined prefill/decode instance, and E/P/D , with all three stages deployed separately. Figure 1. E+PD separates encoding from language-model execution. E/P/D additionally separates prefill and decode. EC connectors deliver encoder embeddings; KV connectors transfer the state between prefill and decode. An image-heavy workload may need more encoder capacity without a corresponding increase in decode capacity. A workload with longer responses may require the opposite. Separating the stages allows operators to adjust their instance counts and execution settings independently, while moving encoder computation off the GPUs serving the language model. Transferring embeddings solves only part of the handoff. The consumer also needs enough information to reconstruct the multimodal input layout: placeholder lengths, image grids, feature lengths, and identifiers linking those positions to the transferred embeddings. A straightforward EPD implementation sends the original media to the encoder, transfers the resulting embeddings through an EC connector, and forwards the original request to P/PD. story|title:agentguard transaction guard.content_excerpt: Transaction guardrails for AI agents that hold crypto wallets - simulate, evaluate against policy + reputation, allow/block/escalate with a signed audit trail. EVM + Solana AgentGuard is a transaction guardrail layer for AI agents that hold crypto wallets. Before an agent signs or broadcasts anything, it submits the proposed transaction to AgentGuard, which simulates it against live chain state, evaluates the simulated effects against an operator-defined policy, and returns allow , block or escalate with a human-readable explanation, a 0–100 risk score and an immutable audit record. Agents never get to decide for themselves whether a transaction is safe. It works on EVM chains and Solana, decodes the usual drain vectors (unlimited approvals, setApprovalForAll , permits, swaps with zero minimum output, SetAuthority, interactions with never-seen contracts), and ships with a conservative default policy plus a TypeScript SDK that wraps any signer so that signTransaction / sendTransaction are checked transparently. On top of the rule engine, a contract reputation layer ( @agentguard/reputation , in this repo) aggregates allow/deny lists, on-chain heuristics (age, proxy, bytecode size) and optional external intel feeds, and an optional behavioral anomaly layer ( @agentguard/behavior , separately licensed, see What's open and what's not ) scores each transaction against the agent's own learned baseline. Both plug into the same pipeline and both fail closed: an outage or an unreadable profile escalates, never allows. Everything in this repository is open source under the Apache License 2.0 : the shared types, the policy engine and default policy, the EVM and Solana simulation adapters, the contract reputation layer, the HTTP API with its tamper-evident audit log, the SDK, the demo and all of the tests. The behavioral anomaly layer is not in this repository. It ships as a separately licensed package, @agentguard/behavior , that learns a per-agent baseline (counterparties, amounts, cadence, approvals) from allowed decisions and flags transactions that are out of character for that agent, for example a $95 transfer to a never-paid address from an agent whose history is 30 routine $5 payments, which no static rule catches. It plugs into the open core without any code change here: The @agentguard/behavior package lives at https://github.com/Radmo3/agentguard-behavior (private; contact the maintainers for licensing). The review was fine. It was a review of different code. I have been doing this for roughly thirty years, and I can report that “the thing we checked is not the thing we shipped” is the oldest bug in the business. We have simply found a way to do it faster and with more confidence. I wrote Uncle ( github.com/unclehq/uncle ) because I got tired of it. At Yahoo I built Yahoo Mail's anti-spam system. Billions of messages a month, six patents, and one durable lesson: a component does not get to declare its own output trustworthy because it produced it. Spammers taught me that. Apparently it also applies to the thing we now let write our code, review our code, and then tell us how it went. Today's workflow: the agent implements, tests, reviews itself, and reports “done, all green.” Did the tests run? Did they finish? Did the reviewer look at the final code? Who knows, ask the agent. (It will say yes. It is very confident. It is always very confident.) A second reviewing agent does not fix this. Adding reviewers to an unbound review is just adding more people to a meeting that has already ended. A Git tree has a hash. That is a concrete thing to staple evidence to. So record that the review passed against a particular tree, that the tests passed against that same tree, that a human approved it, and then check, before publishing, that you are still holding that tree. Here is a real run from a demo project: The last green check is the one that matters here: the tree you are holding, 9edd…fedc , is the tree that was reviewed, so the evidence applies to this code. That is all it tells you. Two lines are red. The verification run failed (one command regressed against the baseline), and the adversarial-review gate was approved by the agent on nobody's behalf, because the run was unattended. Uncle prints both instead of rounding up. Also note the signature line: a signature is present, but with no trust root to check it against, it proves nothing about who signed. Verified , signed and a human looked at it are different claims, and the tool refuses to blur them. Revolutionary, I know. Change the tree and the evidence stops applying. story|title:announcing ga of genie ontol.content_excerpt: The agentic ontology, built by agents, governed by people, and designed for every agent, is now Generally Available with expanded knowledge sources and new tools to curate and refine it. AI agents are only as useful as their understanding of the business in which they work. Within a given domain, teams can curate that understanding by hand. Thousands of customers now run Genie Agents in production this way, including 7-Eleven, Virgin Atlantic and General Motors. However, enterprises are no longer deploying a single agent for a single domain. They are deploying many agents across every function, and each needs the same accurate and complete understanding of how the business works. The enterprise context that agents need is far larger than any team can write down or model by hand. It lives in the logic behind thousands of production dashboards, SQL queries, notebooks and BI semantic models, as well as in the documents and applications where teams record definitions and maintain a working knowledge of who does what. It also changes every week as products launch, campaigns run, and teams reorganize. This is why ontologies have historically struggled in the enterprise. Built by specialists and maintained manually, they captured only a narrow slice of the business and quickly became outdated as the business evolved. Agents change both sides of that problem. They are now the primary consumers of enterprise context, and they can also produce it by learning from the work teams already do. The result is a new kind of agentic ontology, built by agents, used by agents and governed by the people who know the business. We believe every organization will need a single agentic ontology that connects to all of its data, learns continuously from how the business operates and gives every agent the same governed understanding, whether it runs on Databricks or elsewhere. Building context, agent by agent, produces separate and partial views of the business, and those views inevitably conflict. An enterprise ontology should therefore be shared infrastructure that IT and data leaders own in the same way they own the data platform beneath it. story|title:cutting llm token costs with.content_excerpt: Screening news with TypeSafe Jev before LLM synthesis cut input tokens 16–18% at a 0.70 threshold; blind judges could not tell five of six cells from raw. Currents News API keyword search is built for recall. A query for a geopolitical development or a stock ticker returns every publication that mentions the search terms, including wire duplicates, boilerplate press releases, and generic sector watchlists. An agent that summarizes this output pays frontier input prices for every article, on-topic or not, on every scheduled run. The two tiers differ by roughly 50–70× in input-token price. Frontier synthesis input currently runs $2.00–3.00 per million tokens; TypeSafe Jev classification input is $0.042 per million tokens. The practical answer is to move the relevance decision upstream: screen each candidate title and snippet with Jev, and send only retained candidates to the synthesis model. We built this pipeline end-to-end and measured it on live data: 2,000 candidate articles across two real news pools, 60 briefings from three synthesis models, and a blind panel that scored filtered versus raw briefings without knowing which was which. At the default 0.70 relevance threshold, screening cut downstream input tokens by 16–18%; five of six blind-panel quality cells were statistically indistinguishable from raw, and the sixth showed a small negative delta. Stricter thresholds screened out 30–52% of candidates. At frontier pricing, this nets roughly $10–17 per 1,000 screened 200-article batches per synthesis model. One 200-article candidate batch costs a frontier model roughly 35,000–45,000 prompt tokens, and a full 1,000-article pool costs roughly 174,000–223,000 per pass. A scheduled daily pipeline pays that on every run. The cost is not only financial. Tangential commentary and syndication duplicates also consume the model's attention budget and slow generation, because time-to-first-token scales with context length. Three questions determine whether screening helps: how much of a real keyword-search pool is irrelevant, how many tokens removing it saves, and whether the briefing degrades when filtered. story|title:reprogramming dormant neuron.content_excerpt: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns. To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models. Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails. At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected. More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it. The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment. We developed a new enterprise data-agent benchmark in collaboration with Turing to compare Genie with two major frontier agents and their respective harnesses on business questions in a live Databricks workspace. The evaluation measures answer accuracy, token usage and time to complete the task. Genie had a 91% pass rate, compared with 45% and 58% for the other frontier agents, while using fewer than half the tokens. Unlike previous data agent benchmarks that typically only include tables, this benchmark also includes notebooks, dashboards, saved SQL queries, documents, and other analytical assets that capture enterprise knowledge, business definitions, and calculation rules. These assets provide key enterprise context that table schemas alone cannot establish. Genie Ontology is the enterprise context layer that gives every AI agent a shared understanding of the business . It automatically extracts and organizes this knowledge, surfacing relevant context for Genie to use when answering questions. Our previous evaluation of Genie with ontology used a proprietary dataset. This benchmark evaluates Genie using tasks and supporting analytical assets designed for sharing, so others can also run the evaluation. Answering business questions correctly requires accessing the institutional knowledge about how an organization interprets and uses its data. Teams develop this knowledge through everyday analytical work: establishing revenue definitions, maintaining dashboards that reflect current reporting rules, and writing queries that handle business-specific exceptions. The questions in this benchmark require agents to access and reason about this knowledge to perform the tasks correctly. There are already many existing data agent benchmarks, but none that truly emulate real-world usage. We needed a benchmark that tested agents' ability to discover and use business knowledge distributed across notebooks, dashboards, saved SQL queries and other documents. Existing data agent benchmarks mostly focus on a set of tables and the pipeline code that builds them, and the performance on these benchmarks is similar between the agents.
